en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Future Enemies, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi state during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with devas, nāgas, and spirits.

The deities, the sovereign, the ministers, and the common people all went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves, received his teachings, and performed every ritual of offering with the utmost propriety.
When Devadatta witnessed this, his jealousy became boundless, and he returned to tell Prince Ajātaśatru:
"Your father has transported the treasures of the entire kingdom to offer them to the Buddha and the śramaṇas; the state treasury is now utterly depleted."
"You should plan for this early; once you have ascended the throne as king, I shall raise an army to go and subdue the Buddha.
You may be the king and I shall be the Buddha; thus both of us will find our proper place—is this not excellent!"
"You must certainly bring this to fruition.
Before he was even born, Devadatta had already formed this conspiracy with him; he then commanded his powerful ministers to mobilize the troops, decreeing:
"When the King returns, seize his seals and insignia and place him in prison."
When the king returned, the minister immediately followed his orders and placed the king in prison.
The king’s mind remained serene; reflecting upon his past misdeeds, he felt no fear and redoubled his faith in the Buddha’s words.
The King said,
"What transgression have I committed that you should punish me? The Empress,
the ladies of noble rank, and all from the highest to the lowest throughout the land were moved to grief and lamentation.
The King looked back and said to those who were weeping:

"The Buddha has taught that heaven and earth, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the seas, and the mountains—all that comes into being must inevitably perish; that which flourishes will surely decline; that which meets must eventually part; and that which is born must necessarily die."
Because of this, one revolves through the cycle of sorrow and grief without end, leading to profound suffering.
If one seeks its source and examines its beginning, existence arises when causes and conditions converge; this is called birth.
Existence ceases when causes and conditions disperse; this is called emptiness.

The body is merely the four great elements; the soul and spirit of sentient beings dwell within them as a temporary lodging. Upon death, they return to their original source, and the soul and spirit depart into emptiness—this is what is meant by "non-self."
"If one cannot even preserve one's own body, how can one constantly guard a kingdom?
When the Buddha first entered our country, I had no son.
He asked me:"
"Do you know who the future king will be?
I replied, "I do not know."
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"All things are impermanent; contemplate this deeply.
The Buddha’s admonition to me was precisely for this moment.
"Each of you must strive with resolve and cherish the Buddha's admonitions.
The King said to the Crown Prince:
"Whenever you were ill, my heart burned with anxiety; I wished to save you from peril by offering my own life and body in your stead."
"The benevolence and kindness of one's parents is such that Heaven alone is supreme.
With what state of mind do you harbor the resolve to endure such treacherous evil?
One who kills their parents shall die and enter Mount Tai, where they will not find rest; you are certain to suffer this fate."
"I am your honored father; even when one honors and reveres one's own dear parents, one still fears that one's name may not match one's deeds, so how much more so for killing a father?
I bestow this kingdom upon you; I wish to go to the Buddha’s place to become a śramaṇa."
I observe that lust is like fire burning the body; the fondness for women is as empty as space, yet those who lack insight are without exception deluded by it!
Only by beholding the Buddhist scriptures can one illuminate the extreme wickedness of female artifice and realize how worldly glory and profit harm the self.
The Prince said, "Do not speak so much.
I have fulfilled my long-cherished vow; how could there be any pardon?"
The King commanded the prison officials, saying,
"Cut off their food supply so that they may die of starvation.
As the officials were leading them into the prison, King Pingsha turned toward where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with deep reverence, and said:
"Though you possess the evils of heaven and earth, I harbor not even a hair’s breadth of resentment.
I hold only to the Buddha's teaching:
the world has no eternal joy; its suffering is long-lasting."
Entering the prison with his hair disheveled, he looked up to heaven and cried out:
"How painful!
How could Heaven have such a way?"
The Queen, the Consorts, the Noble Ladies, and everyone in the kingdom, high and low alike, were all overcome with grief and lamentation.
The Queen said to the Crown Prince:
"The Great King has been bound in shackles and cast into prison; he must rely on others for every movement, whether sitting or lying down, and his suffering is beyond words."

"Since your birth, Great King, your sincere heart has been suspended upon you; we have not forgotten you even in eating or resting. As the four elements waxed and waned, we lay prostrate beside you, our tears and snot mingling together, our hearts consumed and our bodies withered, wishing to sacrifice our own lives in exchange for yours."
One should maintain the upbringing of gods and humans, never acting in opposition to it.
As the Buddha said in a sutra:
"Among all forms of goodness, nothing is greater than filial piety."
"The greatest of evils is surely to harm one's own kin!
When elders and juniors serve one another, Heaven ought to protect them; how much more so in the case of one's own parents?

You have followed a cruel and tyrannical path and committed this grave evil; you shall certainly enter Mount Tai—where sixty billion years in the world constitute a single day and night—and you shall endure various poisons in every place for many years."
"You must complete this; will it not be difficult?
For those who act to gratify their own desires never fail to regret them later.
The Crown Prince said:
"I have harbored the ambition since my youth to kill my father and become king; today I have attained my wish—what need is there for admonition?
The Queen said, "One who does not heed admonition is laying the foundation for the ruin of a state!"
"I wish to see the Great King; would it not be possible?
The Prince said, "It may be so."

Later, having purified her body through bathing and anointed it with honey and parched grain flour, the queen entered to see the Great King; she did not recognize him, for his face was emaciated and wasted by disease.
She raised a cry of lamentation, and among those who heard it, there were none who did not shed tears. The queen said:
"The Buddha taught that glory and pleasure are impermanent, while the suffering of transgression is constant."
The king said:
“The jailers have cut off my food and drink, and I have been parched with hunger and thirst for many days.
Within my body there are eighty thousand households, and in each household there are several hundred kinds of worms that disturb the interior of my belly.”
"The flesh and blood have been consumed, and my life span is now at its end!
As he spoke, his voice choked with emotion; his breath ceased and then resumed.
The Empress said:
"I fully understand this hardship.
I shall smear my body with flour and honey so that you may eat me;
you must simply reflect upon the Buddha's admonition and not neglect it."
When the king had finished eating, he turned toward where the Buddha was, and with a sobbing voice, he prostrated himself and said:
"The Buddha has taught that honor and fortune are difficult to preserve, being like an illusion and like a dream; this is truly as Your Holiness has instructed!"
He said to the queen:
"When I was king, my realm was vast and my food, clothing, and pleasures were abundant;
now that I am in prison, I shall surely die of starvation."
The perverse teachings you have received run counter to the Buddha’s benevolent instruction.

I do not fear death; my only regret is that I did not personally receive the Buddha’s pure transformation and lecture on the profound mysteries of the Honored Way with Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Mahākāśyapa!
The king spoke again to the queen with gravity:
"The Buddha has said that affection is like various birds gathering to roost in a tree; at dawn they each disperse, according to their respective karmic retributions."

Maudgalyāyana has already eliminated all defilements and extinguished all evils, and having attained the six supernormal powers and the fourfold penetration, he was still beaten by a brahmin out of greed and envy; how much more so, then, would it be for me?
Calamities and evils pursue a person just as a shadow follows the body and an echo responds to a sound.

A Buddha is difficult to encounter in this age, his divine transformations are difficult to hear, and the noble assembly’s lofty conduct and immeasurable rituals are beyond the capacity of worldly scholars to practice.
"Carrying the Buddha's scriptures in his heart, he transformed the people through benevolence;
having obtained the merit of offerings and received this pure transformation, it is indeed truly difficult to encounter such a person!
I am now dying; my spirit shall depart for distant realms."
"Indeed, for those who wish to establish their will, nothing surpasses the Buddha-dharma.
You must guard it carefully to ward off future calamities!
Upon hearing the King’s admonition, the Queen was once again overcome with grief and lamentation.
The Crown Prince interrogated the prison official, saying, "It has been several days since the King was cut off from food; why does he not die?
The official replied:
"The Queen has entered prison; let us offer her parched grain and honey as tribute to prolong the King's life.
The Crown Prince said:
"From this day forward, do not allow the Queen to see the King."
The king was hungry; he rose and prostrated toward where the Buddha was, and immediately his hunger vanished, and the night became bright.
When the prince heard of this, he ordered the windows and doors to be blocked and the soles of his feet to be scraped away, so that the king could not rise and behold the Buddha’s radiance.
The official immediately pared the soles of her feet.
Her pain was immeasurable, yet she did not forget to recollect the Buddha.
From afar, the Buddha preached a sutra for her, saying:
"Indeed, as for good and evil deeds, calamity and fortune return to one's own person;
how can one not be cautious! King Bimbisāra replied, "Even if my body were to be dismembered and cut into pieces, I would never think of evil."
The World-Honored One spoke again:

“I am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha, the Teacher of Gods and Men, the Charioteer of the Dharma. Before me, the suns, moons, devas, and nāgas of the trichiliocosm all bow their heads; yet even those who have harbored residual calamities from past lives do not release them now—how much more so for ordinary people?”

The King, having received the grace of the God among Gods and fully understood his past transgressions, did not dare harbor resentment or expectations, nor did he fear the sin of being burned and boiled by the Great Mountain. With his heart centered on the Buddha and his disciples, he never dared to be negligent whether sitting or lying down; he immediately joined his palms, bowed his head to the ground, and said:
"If my life were to end this very day, the divine transformation would forever cease."
Sobbing and choking with sobs, he was silent for a moment before his breath ceased.
The ministers and citizens of the entire kingdom could not refrain from prostrating themselves in grief, crying out to heaven, "Alas!

King Bimbisāra immediately attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna); he was reborn in the heavens, the three gates to the lower realms were closed, and all sufferings were utterly extinguished!
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Enemies Yet to Be Born.
